title: ORA-00942 Table or View Does Not Exist: Causes and Fixes
description: Fix ORA-00942 table or view does not exist in Oracle: missing schema prefix, grants, role privileges in procedures, quoted names and broken synonyms.
focusKeyword: ora-00942 table or view does not exist

Oracle 19c SQL Language Reference: CREATE SYNONYM
Oracle 23ai SQL Language Reference: DROP TABLE

reviewNotes: All examples written from the 19c/23ai docs and need a test run. Please check: (1) the exact SQL*Plus error layout and asterisk positions, and the LINE/COL values in the SHOW ERRORS output (4/37 is an estimate); (2) whether a synonym to a missing object gives ORA-00942 or ORA-00980 on your version (the article says either may appear); (3) the claim that 23ai+ prints the object name in the message: the official error page documents the 'table or view object_name does not exist' form, and one blog reports a backport to 19.22, which I could not verify, so the article only claims 23ai and later; (4) that the object privilege added to an already-enabled role takes effect without reconnecting (the article hedges with 'if it still fails, reconnect'). The ORA-01031 for UPDATE-with-only-SELECT statement is standard behaviour but not taken from a doc page.

data.text: ORA-00942: table or view does not exist means Oracle could not find the table or view you named, as seen by the user running the statement. Very often the table does exist. The real problem is a missing schema prefix, a missing privilege, a privilege that came through a role inside a stored procedure, or a name created with double quotes.
This guide walks through each cause on a small sample schema. For every cause you get a query to confirm it and the exact fix, so you can stop guessing and go straight to the right one.
What ORA-00942 means

When you write SELECT * FROM orders, Oracle has to turn the name orders into one real object. If you do not give a schema, it looks first for an object called ORDERS in your current schema, and then for a public synonym called ORDERS. If neither exists, or one exists but you have no privilege on it, you get ORA-00942.

That last part surprises people. If the table exists in another schema but you have no privilege on it, Oracle still reports ORA-00942 rather than telling you about the missing grant. The official error reference lists exactly this: the table may not exist, a synonym may point to a missing object, or the user may not have access to it.

data.title: Newer releases show the object name
data.text: The Oracle error reference documents a form of the message that includes the name, written as SCHEMA.OBJECT_NAME when a schema was given. Newer releases (Oracle Database 23ai and later) print that name, which helps a lot when a query joins many tables. In 19c you usually see only ORA-00942: table or view does not exist with an asterisk under the failing name.
Sample setup

We use two users. SALES owns the data. APP_USER is the account an application logs in with. Run the first block as a DBA user (in a multitenant database, connect to your pluggable database, not the root).

data.caption: Create the two users and a role (run as DBA)
Create the ORDERS table as SALES

data.text: If your database has no USERS tablespace, change the QUOTA line to a tablespace that exists.
Step 1: find out whether the object exists, and who owns it
Before changing anything, ask the dictionary. Run this as a DBA (or any user with access to DBA_OBJECTS):

data.caption: Search every schema for the name

data.text: Output (expected output). The table exists and SALES owns it. Now run the same check as the failing user, using ALL_OBJECTS, which only lists objects that user can access:

data.code:
-- Connected as APP_USER
SELECT owner, object_name, object_type
  FROM all_objects
 WHERE UPPER(object_name) = 'ORDERS';
data.caption: What the failing user can see

data.code: no rows selected
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: This comparison tells you a lot. If the DBA sees the table but the user sees nothing, it is a privilege problem. If nobody sees it, the object really is missing, or its name is not what you think. Using UPPER(object_name) also catches tables created with mixed-case quoted names.
Cause 1: no privilege on the table
APP_USER tries to read the orders using the full name, before any grant is in place:

data.code: SELECT * FROM sales.orders;
data.caption: Run as APP_USER

data.code:
SELECT * FROM sales.orders
                    *
ERROR at line 1:
ORA-00942: table or view does not exist
data.caption: Output (expected output, SQL*Plus on 19c)

data.text: The schema is right and the table exists, yet the error is the same. Oracle needs a privilege before it will resolve the name for you. Connect as SALES and grant SELECT through the role we created:

data.code:
-- Connected as SALES
GRANT SELECT ON orders TO orders_reader;
data.caption: Grant through a role

data.text: Now SELECT * FROM sales.orders returns the three rows as APP_USER. If it still fails, reconnect so the session picks up its roles. To check what a user has been granted on a table, query USER_TAB_PRIVS as that user (direct grants) and ROLE_TAB_PRIVS (grants through enabled roles):

data.caption: Privileges APP_USER gets through roles

data.text: Output (expected output). Keep this in mind: SELECT only. If APP_USER now tries an UPDATE on the table it can see, Oracle reports a privilege error (ORA-01031: insufficient privileges) instead, because the name now resolves.
Cause 2: the table is in another schema
Now APP_USER has the privilege, but the application code says only ORDERS:

data.code: SELECT * FROM orders;
data.caption: Run as APP_USER, no schema prefix

data.code:
SELECT * FROM orders
              *
ERROR at line 1:
ORA-00942: table or view does not exist
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: Oracle looked for APP_USER.ORDERS and then for a public synonym called ORDERS. It found neither, so it never looked in SALES. You have three fixes. Pick one per application, not a mix.
Fix A: qualify the name

data.code: SELECT * FROM sales.orders;
data.caption: Clear and explicit

data.text: Fix B: create a private synonym

data.caption: The synonym maps ORDERS to SALES.ORDERS

data.text: Output (expected output). A synonym is only a name. It does not grant anything, so the SELECT privilege from Cause 1 is still required.
Fix C: change the current schema for the session

data.code:
ALTER SESSION SET CURRENT_SCHEMA = sales;

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;
data.caption: Unqualified names now resolve in SALES

data.text: Unqualified names now resolve in SALES for this session. This is handy in a logon trigger or a connection pool setup. It changes name resolution only. Privileges are still checked against APP_USER.
Cause 3: it works in SQL but fails inside a procedure
This is the case behind most "ORA-00942 but table exists" searches. APP_USER can query SALES.ORDERS in SQL*Plus, so it writes a procedure that does the same:

data.caption: Run as APP_USER

data.code:
Warning: Procedure created with compilation errors.

Errors for PROCEDURE COUNT_ORDERS:

LINE/COL ERROR
-------- ------------------------------------------------
4/3      PL/SQL: SQL Statement ignored
4/37     PL/SQL: ORA-00942: table or view does not exist
data.caption: Output (expected output, line and column numbers may differ)

data.text: Why this happens

The privilege came through the role ORDERS_READER. A procedure is a definer's rights unit by default. The PL/SQL Language Reference explains that when such a unit runs, Oracle switches to the owner's privileges and enables only the role PUBLIC. Static SQL is also checked when the procedure is compiled, and at compile time every unit is treated as definer's rights. So any privilege that arrives only through a role (other than PUBLIC) is invisible to compiled PL/SQL.
The fix: grant the privilege directly

data.caption: Direct grant, then recompile

data.code:
Procedure altered.

Orders: 3

PL/SQL procedure successfully completed.
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.title: AUTHID CURRENT_USER is not a shortcut
data.text: Adding AUTHID CURRENT_USER does not fix the compile error. The docs state that static SQL is checked at compile time as if the unit were definer's rights, so the owner still needs a direct grant. Switching to dynamic SQL with EXECUTE IMMEDIATE only moves the check to run time. Grant the privilege directly instead of working around it.

The same rule applies to triggers, functions, packages and views that the owner creates on top of another schema's tables. If an object compiles fine as the DBA but not as the real owner, look for role-only grants first.
Cause 4: the table was created with a quoted name
Some tools and migration scripts generate names in double quotes. Oracle stores unquoted names in uppercase, but a quoted name is kept exactly as typed and becomes case sensitive.

data.code:
-- Connected as SALES
CREATE TABLE "Payments" (
  payment_id NUMBER,
  amount     NUMBER(10,2)
);

SELECT * FROM payments;    -- looks for PAYMENTS: ORA-00942
SELECT * FROM "Payments";  -- works
data.caption: A mixed-case quoted name

data.text: The first query fails because payments is read as PAYMENTS, and no table has that name. The second works because the quotes match the stored name exactly. You can spot such tables with the Step 1 query: the OBJECT_NAME column shows the mixed case.
The lasting fix is to rename the table to an ordinary uppercase name, after checking that nothing depends on the old one:

data.code: ALTER TABLE "Payments" RENAME TO payments;
data.caption: Rename to a normal, case-insensitive name

data.text: Oracle's own documentation recommends against quoted identifiers for object names for this reason.
Cause 5: a synonym points to a missing object

Oracle lets you create a synonym for an object that does not exist yet, and a synonym is left behind when its table is dropped or renamed. Queries through it then fail. Depending on the case you may see ORA-00942 or ORA-00980 (synonym translation is no longer valid). Check where the synonym points:

data.caption: Where does the synonym lead?

data.text: Output (expected output). Then confirm that TABLE_OWNER.TABLE_NAME exists with the Step 1 query. If the synonym uses a database link, the name is resolved and the privilege is checked on the remote database, for the user the link connects as, so run the checks there.
Cause 6: DROP in a script when the table is not there
Install and test scripts often start by dropping a table. If it is missing, the DROP raises ORA-00942 and many script runners stop.

In Oracle Database 23ai and later you can write DROP TABLE IF EXISTS orders_stage;, which drops the table only if it exists. In 19c and earlier, catch only this one error code and re-raise everything else:

data.caption: Ignore ORA-00942 only, on 19c and earlier

data.text: Never swallow every error here. A failed DROP for any other reason, such as a lock or a privilege problem, should still stop the script.
Common mistakes

items.content: Granting to a role and testing only in SQL*Plus. The query works interactively, then the package fails to compile. Grant directly to any user that owns PL/SQL or views which use the table.
Checking USER_TABLES as the wrong user. USER_TABLES shows only your own tables. Use ALL_OBJECTS as the failing user and DBA_OBJECTS as a DBA, and compare.
Creating a synonym and expecting it to grant access. A synonym only maps a name. The privilege on the underlying table is still required.
Running in the wrong container or database. In a multitenant database, the table lives in a PDB. Connected to CDB$ROOT, the PDB's tables are not visible. Check with SHOW CON_NAME in SQL*Plus.
Using GRANT SELECT ANY TABLE to make the error go away. It hides the real problem and gives far more access than needed. Grant on the specific object.

data.text: Best practices to avoid ORA-00942

items.content: Pick one naming strategy per application: always qualify schema names, or use private synonyms, or set CURRENT_SCHEMA at logon.
Give roles to people who run ad hoc queries, and direct object grants to schemas that own code.
Never use quoted mixed-case names for tables and columns.
Keep grants in the same deployment script as the CREATE TABLE, so a new environment never misses them.
When an application reports ORA-00942, log the full SQL text. In a join of ten tables, the statement and the error position are what tell you which name failed.

data.text: Frequently asked questions
Why do I get ORA-00942 when the table exists?

Because the user running the statement cannot see it. Either the table is in another schema and you did not prefix it, the user has no privilege on it, the privilege comes only through a role and you are inside PL/SQL, or the table name was created in quotes with mixed case.
How do I fix ORA-00942 in a stored procedure?

Grant the needed privilege directly to the procedure owner, for example GRANT SELECT ON sales.orders TO app_user;, and recompile the procedure. Roles other than PUBLIC are not enabled when definer's rights PL/SQL is compiled or run.
Does ORA-00942 mean I need a GRANT?

Not always, but often. If DBA_OBJECTS shows the table and ALL_OBJECTS for the failing user does not, a grant is missing. If DBA_OBJECTS shows nothing, the object really does not exist under that name.
What is the difference between ORA-00942 and ORA-01031?

ORA-00942 means the name could not be resolved to an object you can access. ORA-01031 (insufficient privileges) means Oracle found the object, but you lack the specific privilege for the operation, for example UPDATE when you only have SELECT.
Summary

items.content: Run the Step 1 checks: DBA_OBJECTS as a DBA, ALL_OBJECTS as the failing user.
Prefix the schema, create a synonym, or set CURRENT_SCHEMA when the table lives elsewhere.
Grant the specific privilege on the table, not an ANY privilege.
For procedures, packages, triggers and views, grant directly to the owner, not through a role.
Look for quoted mixed-case names and rename them.
Check ALL_SYNONYMS when a synonym is involved.
Use DROP TABLE IF EXISTS on 23ai, or catch only SQLCODE -942 on older releases.

linkedin.post:
Your SELECT works in SQL Developer, but the same query inside a procedure fails with ORA-00942. The table is right there.

ORA-00942 rarely means the table is gone. It means the user running the statement cannot see it.

The usual causes:
1. No schema prefix. Oracle looks in your own schema and in public synonyms only. Write sales.orders or create a synonym.
2. No privilege. Without a grant, Oracle reports ORA-00942, not a privilege error.
3. Grant came through a role. Definer's rights PL/SQL enables only PUBLIC, so the procedure owner needs a direct GRANT.
4. Quoted names. CREATE TABLE "Payments" is case sensitive, so SELECT * FROM payments fails.
5. Broken synonym. Check ALL_SYNONYMS to see where it points.

Quick test: compare DBA_OBJECTS (as DBA) with ALL_OBJECTS (as the failing user). If only the DBA sees the table, a grant is missing.

Which one cost you the most time: the role grant or the missing schema prefix?
